title: Generic classes, methods, bounded types, wildcards, PECS rule
shortTitle: Generic classes, methods, bounded types, wildcards, PECS rule

s1_definition.profdef: Generics add **compile-time type safety** to collections and classes. Without generics: `List list = new ArrayList(); list.add("text"); Integer n = (Integer) list.get(0)` → `ClassCastException` at RUNTIME. With generics: `List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(); list.add("text"); Integer n = list.get(0)` → **COMPILE ERROR** (caught before running!). **Generic class**: `class Box<T> { T item; }`. **Generic method**: `<T> T first(List<T> list)`. **Bounded type**: `<T extends Number>` restricts T to Number subclasses. **Wildcards**: `? extends T` (upper bound — PRODUCER, read-only) vs `? super T` (lower bound — CONSUMER, write-only). **PECS**: Producer-Extends, Consumer-Super.
s1_definition.analogy: Without generics: a filing drawer accepts ANYTHING (cheques, cash, forms, lunch boxes). You reach in expecting a cheque → grab a lunch box → CRASH (ClassCastException). With generics: drawer labeled `<Cheque>` — compiler rejects anything that isn't a cheque at FILING TIME (compile time), not at retrieval time. PECS: `? extends Account` = "I will READ accounts from this (producer)" — could be SavingsAccount, CurrentAccount. `? super SavingsAccount` = "I will PUT savings accounts into this (consumer)" — could be a List<Account> or List<Object>.
s1_definition.oneliner: Generics = compile-time type safety (no runtime ClassCastException). `<T extends Number>` = bounded. PECS: `? extends T` = read/produce. `? super T` = write/consume.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Generics add **compile-time type safety** to collections and classes. Without generics: `List list = new ArrayList(); list.add("text"); Integer n = (Integer) list.get(0)` → `ClassCastException` at RUNTIME. With generics: `List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(); list.add("text"); Integer n = list.get(0)` → **COMPILE ERROR** (caught before running!). **Generic class**: `class Box<T> { T item; }`. **Generic method**: `<T> T first(List<T> list)`. **Bounded type**: `<T extends Number>` restricts T to Number subclasses. **Wildcards**: `? extends T` (upper bound — PRODUCER, read-only) vs `? super T` (lower bound — CONSUMER, write-only). **PECS**: Producer-Extends, Consumer-Super.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Without generics: a filing drawer accepts ANYTHING (cheques, cash, forms, lunch boxes). You reach in expecting a cheque → grab a lunch box → CRASH (ClassCastException). With generics: drawer labeled `<Cheque>` — compiler rejects anything that isn't a cheque at FILING TIME (compile time), not at retrieval time. PECS: `? extends Account` = "I will READ accounts from this (producer)" — could be SavingsAccount, CurrentAccount. `? super SavingsAccount` = "I will PUT savings accounts into this (consumer)" — could be a List<Account> or List<Object>.

**One line to remember:** Generics = compile-time type safety (no runtime ClassCastException). `<T extends Number>` = bounded. PECS: `? extends T` = read/produce. `? super T` = write/consume.

sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India, the engineering team hit a real problem that maps directly onto generic classes, bounded types and the PECS rule. Rajesh (account SAV2001, a software engineer with a savings balance of 1,000,000 rupees) and Priya (account CUR3001, a property owner with a current balance of 250,000 rupees) both run operations that stress the system's collection handling, and the wrong data-structure choice here caused slow lookups, lost entries, or incorrect ordering in production reports.

The mini-project below reproduces that banking scenario and shows exactly how generic classes, bounded types and the PECS rule solves it correctly, using BigDecimal for every money value and the same Account model with debit and credit behaviour.
sections.s5_journey:
The input is a generic `Repository<T>` and bounded methods that process accounts following the PECS rule.

**Step 1.** A bounded method `<T extends Account> void process(List<T> accounts)` accepts Rajesh's savings and Priya's current accounts because both extend Account.

**Step 2.** A producer parameter `List<? extends Account>` is used only to read accounts out, while a consumer parameter `List<? super SavingsAccount>` is used only to add into, matching "Producer Extends, Consumer Super".

**Step 3.** The compiler enforces these wildcard rules so the data flows in the right direction, letting accounts be read and written safely without any unchecked cast.
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Input: Rajesh SAV2001 (Rs.1,000,000), Priya CUR3001 (Rs.250,000)
    │
    ▼
  Service layer (applies generic classes, bounded types and the PECS rule)
    │  loads accounts into the collection
    │  performs the operation (add / lookup / order / dedup)
    ▼
  Collection state changes
    │  SAV2001 and CUR3001 processed with BigDecimal amounts
    ▼
  Output: correct result returned to the caller
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Generics provide compile-time type safety — errors caught at compilation, not runtime ClassCastException. Generic classes (`class Box<T>`), methods (`<T> T find()`), bounded types (`<T extends Number>` restricts T). PECS rule: Producer-Extends (read from `List<? extends Number>` — could be Integer, Double), Consumer-Super (write to `List<? super Integer>` — could be List<Number>, List<Object>). Type erasure: generics exist only at compile time — at runtime, `List<String>` becomes `List` (raw). This is why you can't do `new T()` or `instanceof List<String>`.
